candidates.title: Over Your Shoulder
candidates.pitch: An essay about attention opens with a doorbell; how long and how rhythmically the visitor presses it is the page's first guess at them. As they read, the page quietly measures dwell time per paragraph, scroll reversals, pointer stillness and tab-aways, then shows a hedged margin note ('you slowed down here, about 60 percent sure') and rewrites later paragraphs to mirror the reader: shorter for skimmers, echoing for re-readers, footnoted for lingerers. It ends with a generated reading portrait and a shareable hash, and the fun is performing as a different reader on purpose to collect all the portraits.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless. Form-breaking early-web spirit: the interface is the content, and the rule (the page adapts to how you read it, nothing leaves the device) is felt within ten seconds.

research.summary: Net art of the 1990s made the browser's own layers the subject: JODI projects expose code and fake error screens as primary content, and one 1998 piece redirects the browser so its history list becomes a visible pattern. Modern weird-web examples react to the viewer (blink-triggered warping, text that scrambles under the mouse), but I found none that reads reading itself and rewrites the essay accordingly. The honest science: a CHI 2012 eye-tracking study (36 subjects, 32 tasks) found cursor and gaze only sometimes align, with reading, hesitating and scrolling meaning different things. So the page will present its inferences as hedged guesses and admit when it is wrong, which becomes part of its voice.

sources.title: Web Work: A History of Internet Art (Artforum)
sources.snippet: Artforum's history of internet art, as summarised in a search result, notes that in many JODI projects the exposed programming forms the primary content, making the hidden layer of a page the subject.
sources.note: Establishes interface and code as content in early net art.

sources.title: artelectronicmedia.com (Shanken account of JODI)
sources.snippet: A quoted account describes a 1999 visit to jodi.org returning a mock error message, and a 404 page whose live links lead into other parts of the site.
sources.note: Second independent result: errors and browser behaviour as artistic material.

sources.title: Upstream's Daily Net Art Update (#10)
sources.snippet: Gallery text on ASDFG (1998): the browser is continually redirected from page to page so the visitor's history list becomes a visible pattern.
sources.note: Precedent for a page that uses the visitor's browsing trace as material. Single result.

sources.title: User See, User Point: Gaze and Cursor Alignment in Web Search (Microsoft Research, CHI 2012)
sources.snippet: Eye-tracking study with 36 subjects and 32 search tasks questions the assumption that gaze is well approximated by the cursor; cursor behaviours such as reading, hesitating, scrolling and clicking carry different meaning.
sources.note: Shapes the design: cursor is a weak, conditional proxy for gaze, so the page hedges. Same-organisation PDF also seen, so counted as one source.

sources.title: this website changes every time you blink (Vice)
sources.snippet: Coverage of a site that warps when the viewer's eyes close; the result summary lists other reactive weird sites, some that scramble text under the mouse and one that fades text if you do not blink.
sources.note: Shows reactive-to-viewer sites exist but rely on webcam or simple triggers; summary was blended across results.

sources.title: My Boyfriend Came Back from the War (ACMI)
sources.snippet: A 1996 browser-based work by Olia Lialina in which each click splits the frame into smaller frames until the screen is a mosaic of empty black frames, telling a nonlinear story.
sources.note: Precedent for story told by the browser frame itself; several secondary accounts agreed but the summary was blended.

facts.claim: Per Artforum and a quoted account of jodi.org, JODI works treat exposed code and mock error messages as primary content, as of the sources seen on 2026-10-12.
As of 2026-10-12, per Upstream Gallery, the 1998 work ASDFG redirects the browser page to page so the visitor's history list becomes a visible pattern.
As of 2026-10-12, per Microsoft Research (CHI 2012), a study of 36 subjects on 32 search tasks found gaze and cursor only sometimes aligned, so the cursor is a conditional proxy for gaze.
As of 2026-10-12, per ACMI, Olia Lialina's 1996 'My Boyfriend Came Back from the War' splits browser frames with each click until the screen becomes a mosaic of black frames.

inspirations: My Boyfriend Came Back from the War

design.coreLoop: Ring the doorbell, read a paragraph, see the margin guess, then read the next paragraph that has been chosen from hand-written variants by the running reader model. Pass 1 teaches the rule; pass 2 is play: the visitor performs a reader (skimmer, rereader, lingerer, restless, deliberate) to steer the text and collects distinct portraits and endings. Each portrait is a deterministic canvas glyph of six numbers, so it can be compared and shared through the URL hash.
sophisticationHooks: Reader model: dwell per word, scroll reversals, pointer stillness and horizontal sweeps, tab-away, touch dwell, each blended into five bounded scores with documented thresholds and decay
Variant text: each paragraph has 3 hand-written versions selected deterministically from the profile, so behaviour is testable with simulated readers
Honest hedging: confidence shown as words and bars, with a visible 'I was wrong about you' moment when the profile flips, grounded in the cursor-vs-gaze research
Reading portrait: seeded canvas glyph plus archetype name and hash export; doorbell ring rhythm synthesised procedurally
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: doorbell opener with procedural chime, 8 short paragraphs with 3 variants each (about 1,400 words of copy), reader-model module with simulated-reader test hook, margin-note engine, portrait canvas renderer, hash codec, keyboard path (j/k, space, dwell by key rhythm), a manual 'tell the page how you read' panel for screen-reader and no-pointer users, about/making-of panel. Cut: any webcam or eye tracking, any storage of behaviour, multi-essay support.
risks: Privacy perception: the page must state plainly that nothing is stored or sent and no camera or microphone is used; keep all measurements in memory only.
Cursor-as-gaze is unreliable (CHI 2012 result is search-only, unverified here): the page shows it as 'as of 2026-10-12, per Microsoft Research' and treats every inference as a guess.
Touch and keyboard readers lack pointer signals: fall back to scroll velocity and dwell, and provide the manual panel.
Copy volume (24 variant paragraphs) is the schedule risk: write 5 paragraphs fully first, then expand.
Reduced motion: text mutation must fade or swap without animation when requested.

candidates.title: Tolls In Kind
candidates.pitch: A short, sincere essay about how web pages learned to charge for attention sits behind a run of toll gates, and none of them take money. Each gate asks for payment in kind (patience, dignity, spare seconds, a held-still cursor) behind a sign that lies in one specific, learnable way: a decline button worded as a guilt trip, a price list that quietly inverts, fine print that is the real exit. Spot the rule and the toll drops; misread it and the price rises. Each cleared gate unlocks the next paragraph and a codex card naming the trick, and the run ends with an itemised receipt and a daily seed to compare.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless satire of consent banners and paywalls, owed to the humor slot this week. The form-breaking twist is that the interface is the joke and the essay is the prize.

research.summary: Deceptive-design patterns are well catalogued: several taxonomies exist (Brignull's list with confirmshaming and roach motels; the nagging, obstruction and sneaking grouping used in academic work; the European Data Protection Board's six categories), which gives the gates a real, named rule set to parody. Games about hostile cookie banners already exist (a Berlin university arcade game and a hackathon for the most annoying banners), so this idea differs by making every gate a small hidden-rule puzzle with a different toll currency, gating an actual essay, and by naming the real trick afterwards in a codex.

sources.title: Beat the Cookie Monster (arcade game, Freie Universitaet Berlin)
sources.snippet: Event report on an arcade game where players must reject deceptive cookie banners; a wrong agreement costs one of three lives.
sources.note: Prior art for banner-rejection as a game; defines what to differentiate from.

sources.title: Wasp most-annoying cookie banner hackathon (OpenSaaS blog)
sources.snippet: A blog post about asking users to build the most irritating cookie banners, with community voting; entries include a find-all-the-cookies hidden-element gag.
sources.note: Second independent result that parodies of hostile banners are a known playful genre.

sources.title: 10 dark patterns in ux design (Bejamas)
sources.snippet: Practitioner overview of common dark patterns; the search summary credits Brignull with coining the term and listing 12 categories including confirmshaming and roach motels.
sources.note: Source for the pattern vocabulary; the count of 12 came from a blended summary.

sources.title: Dark Patterns Deceptive Design (University of Washington course slides)
sources.snippet: Course slides grouping patterns into nagging, obstruction and sneaking, with nagging defined as repeated interruption during normal interactions.
sources.note: Gives gate families a taxonomy; single result for this grouping.

sources.title: The Most Annoying UX Patterns of the Modern Web. Part 1 (UX Planet)
sources.snippet: Article listing familiar irritating web patterns, relevant as a source of recognisable gate behaviours for parody.
sources.note: Supports the idea that the targets are widely recognised; I did not see its body text.

sources.title: A Comprehensive Study on Dark Patterns (arXiv)
sources.snippet: A 2024 arXiv study that tabulates dark pattern types under categories such as nagging, obstruction and sneaking, with severity ratings.
sources.note: Academic backing for the category grouping; exact labels not seen.

facts.claim: As of 2026-10-12, a Freie Universitaet Berlin event report and an OpenSaaS blog post each describe games or contests built around deliberately hostile cookie banners, so the genre exists and this idea must differ from it.
As of 2026-10-12, per a University of Washington slide deck, dark patterns are grouped into nagging, obstruction and sneaking.
As of 2026-10-12, per Bejamas, the term dark patterns was coined by a UX designer who listed categories such as confirmshaming and roach motel (the count of 12 is unconfirmed).

design.coreLoop: A gate appears with a sign and a price in a play currency. The visitor reads the sign for the lie (which button is real, which number inverts, where the exit hides), pays, negotiates or finds the loophole, and the paragraph behind the gate is revealed. Gates come from 8 rule families, seeded by the URL hash, so each run reshuffles the tricks and prices. The loop rewards the second minute (recognising a family) and the tenth (reading faster for a lower receipt and filling the codex).
sophisticationHooks: Seeded gate generator: 8 rule families by 3 skins each, with price curves that rise on a misread and fall on a correct read, deterministic from the hash
Three play currencies (patience, dignity, spare seconds) with different spend mechanics; explicitly no real money or payment fields
Codex that names the real trick after each gate, tying the joke to the documented taxonomy with 'as of' dating
Itemised receipt and daily-seed compare, with an always-visible 'skip with shame' escape hatch that logs a costume-drama penalty
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: 8 gate families with 3 skins each (24 short interactions, each solvable in under 15 seconds), seeded generator, wallet and receipt, 8-paragraph essay, codex with localStorage (try/catch, optional), keyboard and touch alternatives for every gate, about/making-of panel. Cut: sound beyond a few procedural blips, multiplayer, any real payment look-alike, any real brand or banner imitation.
risks: Prior art: banner-rejection games exist (FU Berlin, Wasp hackathon); differentiate through hidden-rule puzzles, the essay prize and the codex.
Frustration by design can tip into just being annoying: cap each gate's time, add the skip-with-shame hatch, keep the tone warm.
Accessibility: hold-still and timing gates need non-motor alternatives and reduced-motion variants.
Humor-satire/game neighbours in today's pool (the carried-over Breaking Changes idea) share the satire tone; this one is a puzzle in the weird-experimental category with different form.
Pattern-taxonomy claims are search-only; the codex shows them as 'as of 2026-10-12, per <source>' and avoids the unconfirmed count of 12.
No real company banners or logos: all brands invented, all marks drawn.
